patient.history_present_illness: A 58-year-old man with known alcoholic cirrhosis was brought to the emergency department by his neighbor after being found confused and combative at home. According to the neighbor, the patient had been complaining of dark, tarry stools for approximately 24 hours prior to presentation. He was found sitting in a chair, unable to recognize his neighbor and shouting incoherently. Over the past few days, the patient had reportedly stopped eating, was not taking his lactulose as prescribed, and had continued drinking alcohol. His neighbor noted that his abdomen appeared more distended than usual. He had no known history of seizures or head trauma. On arrival to the ED, the patient was oriented only to his name, was agitated and pulling at IV lines, and could not provide a coherent history. He smelled strongly of alcohol. His skin was visibly jaundiced. He was tachycardic and hypotensive on arrival. Blood was noted on rectal exam, confirming active lower GI blood loss. No focal neurological deficits were identified on initial assessment, and there was no evidence of meningismus. The patient's daughter, reached by phone, confirmed he had a history of hepatic encephalopathy once before, two years ago following a GI bleed, which resolved with lactulose and rifaximin. She reported he had been increasingly confused over the past 48 hours and had refused to go to the hospital until his neighbor forced the issue today.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III), acute-on-chronic, alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 18) — precipitated by GI hemorrhage, hypokalemia, recent alcohol use, and lactulose non-adherence.

optimal_actions.action: Send targeted laboratory studies: CBC, CMP, ammonia, magnesium, lactate, coagulation. Confirms liver dysfunction and screens for precipitants.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia elevated; Hgb low + BUN high (GI bleed marker); K low; cirrhosis features.

optimal_actions.action: Non-contrast CT head — exclude structural alternate cause of AMS (hemorrhage, large stroke, mass) before any LP.
Literature/guideline search to confirm West Haven grading, precipitant management, and lactulose/rifaximin dosing (Multifactorial HE management; variceal bleed; AASLD/EASL).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AASLD/EASL 2014 guidance retrieved; West Haven criteria and precipitant-driven management framework confirmed.

optimal_actions.action: Drug-interaction and medication-reconciliation review covering lactulose, rifaximin, propranolol (HOLD if active bleed/hypotension); avoid sedatives; flag any CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antiemetics, antihistamines) and confirm lactulose/rifaximin dosing in liver disease.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sedating/CNS-depressant medications identified; lactulose and rifaximin reviewed for hepatic dose adjustment.

optimal_actions.action: EEG — characterize and exclude NCSE. Triphasic waves are classic but non-specific (metabolic encephalopathies broadly); main role is exclusion of non-convulsive status epilepticus where the differential supports it.
Consult GI for endoscopy; hepatology — coordinate definitive care, transplant candidacy assessment where applicable.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hepatology / critical-care guidance integrated into management.

optimal_actions.action: Draw two sets of blood cultures, aerobic and anaerobic, before the first antimicrobial dose
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Growth identifies the organism and its susceptibility; a negative or pending culture does not exclude the diagnosis, and yield falls once treatment has started

optimal_actions.action: Perform a diagnostic paracentesis and send ascitic fluid for cell count with differential, protein and culture, inoculating blood-culture bottles at the bedside
optimal_actions.expected_finding: A polymorphonuclear count at or above 250 cells/mm3 establishes spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, which is a precipitant that must be treated whether or not fever or leucocytosis is present

optimal_actions.action: Send urine for microscopy and culture as part of the infection screen
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Pyuria and bacteriuria identify a urinary source; a negative result removes it from the list of precipitants

useless_tools.rationale: Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

sequence_constraints.reason: In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect / hemorrhage on imaging before LP to avoid herniation risk.

critical_actions: Upper endoscopy with variceal banding if bleeding source confirmed.
IV ceftriaxone for SBP prophylaxis in bleeding cirrhotic.
Lactulose enemas / NG; rifaximin via NG.
IV K repletion and thiamine before any dextrose.
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Do not transfuse aggressively to normal Hgb (rebleeding risk).
key_reasoning_points: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
When multiple precipitants coexist, all must be addressed simultaneously — fixing one in isolation will not resolve HE.
